title: A visit to the doctor
paragraphs: Last Monday, Kamila Seitkali woke up feeling terrible. Her head was pounding, her throat was sore, and she had a high temperature of 38.5 degrees. She also had a blocked nose, a dry cough, and she felt completely exhausted. She had not slept well for two nights. Kamila knew immediately that she was not well enough to attend her morning lecture on Economics.

She sent a message to her group chat: "I'm not coming to university today. I've got a fever and I feel awful. Please send me the lecture notes." Her friend Amir replied immediately: "Go to the medical centre — don't wait! You've got to see a doctor." Kamila agreed. She put on her warm coat, wrapped a scarf around her neck, and walked slowly to the WKU Student Medical Centre, which is located on the ground floor of Building 3.

At the reception desk, a friendly nurse named Gulnara asked Kamila to complete a short form. Kamila wrote down her student ID, her group number, her date of birth, and described her symptoms. The nurse took her temperature, her blood pressure, and her pulse. "Your temperature is 38.7 — that is quite high," said Nurse Gulnara. "The doctor will see you in about fifteen minutes."

The doctor's name was Dr. Serik Akhmetov. He was a calm, experienced man in his forties with kind eyes and a reassuring voice. He asked Kamila a series of questions: "How long have you felt this way? Have you got a headache? Does your chest hurt when you breathe? Have you got any allergies? Have you taken any medicine already?" Kamila answered each question carefully and honestly.

After examining her, Dr. Akhmetov explained the diagnosis clearly: "You have got a viral respiratory infection — what we often call a common cold, but quite a serious one. Your body needs rest, warmth, and fluids above all. You don't have to go to hospital — this is not that serious — but you absolutely have to stay home for at least three days." He also told her to drink at least two litres of water per day, to eat hot soup if possible, and to avoid cold air and draughts.

Dr. Akhmetov wrote a prescription for two medicines: an antiviral tablet and a throat spray. He also wrote an official medical note — called a "sick note" or "excuse letter" — for the university. "Give this to your group coordinator," he said. "All your absences will be officially excused." He also strongly advised her to get a flu vaccination before next winter, as this type of infection was very common among students living in dormitories.

On her way back to the dormitory, Kamila stopped at the university pharmacy to collect her medicines. The pharmacist, a young woman named Ainur, explained exactly how to take the tablets: "Take one tablet twice a day — in the morning after breakfast and in the evening after dinner. Do not take them on an empty stomach. And the throat spray — use it three times a day: morning, afternoon, and evening. Shake the bottle well before each use."

Kamila spent the next three days in her dormitory room. Her roommate Zhibek took very good care of her — she brought hot tea with honey and lemon, cooked warm porridge, and made sure Kamila took her medicines on time. By Thursday, Kamila's temperature had returned to normal, her headache was gone, and she felt much stronger. She sent a message to the group chat: "Back on Friday! Thanks for the notes, everyone. Health is truly the most important thing. Take care of yourselves!" 💪

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Akhmetov
dialogue.text: Good morning. Please, take a seat. What brings you to the clinic today?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Good morning, doctor. I've got a headache, a sore throat, and a fever. I feel awful.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Akhmetov
dialogue.text: I see. How long have you had these symptoms?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Since Sunday night — so about two days now. I also have a cough and a blocked nose.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Akhmetov
dialogue.text: Have you got any pain in your chest or difficulty breathing?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: No, just a little tightness sometimes. But my throat is very painful when I swallow.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Akhmetov
dialogue.text: I'm going to check your throat. Open wide, please. Hmm. Yes, it's quite red and inflamed.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Is it serious? I have an important test on Friday.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Akhmetov
dialogue.text: It's a viral infection — quite common this season. But you have to rest properly. No university for three days.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Three days?! I've got so many classes...

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Akhmetov
dialogue.text: I understand. But if you don't rest now, you could be ill for two weeks. The choice is yours.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: You're right, doctor. I'll stay home. Can you give me a medical note for the university?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Akhmetov
dialogue.text: Of course. And drink plenty of water — at least two litres a day. Hot soup is excellent too.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Thank you, doctor. I'll follow all your advice.

vocab.definition: a sign that you are ill or have a health problem
vocab.example: A sore throat is a common symptom of a cold.

vocab.definition: a body temperature that is higher than normal (above 37.5°C)
vocab.example: She has a fever of 38.7 degrees.

vocab.definition: a written order from a doctor for medicine
vocab.example: The doctor wrote a prescription for two medicines.

vocab.definition: the identification of an illness after examining a patient
vocab.example: The diagnosis was a viral respiratory infection.

vocab.definition: extremely tired; having no energy at all
vocab.example: She felt completely exhausted after two sleepless nights.

vocab.definition: red, swollen, and painful, usually because of infection
vocab.example: Her throat was very red and inflamed.

vocab.definition: a shop where medicines are prepared and sold
vocab.example: She collected her medicines from the university pharmacy.

vocab.definition: an injection that protects you from a disease
vocab.example: The doctor advised her to get a flu vaccination.

vocab.definition: an illness caused by bacteria or a virus entering your body
vocab.example: She had a viral respiratory infection.

vocab.definition: a careful check of a patient's body by a doctor
vocab.example: After examining her, the doctor explained the diagnosis.

vocab.definition: a medicine that kills bacteria and treats infections
vocab.example: Antibiotics do not work against viral infections.

vocab.definition: the process of becoming well again after illness
vocab.example: By Thursday, Kamila's recovery was almost complete.

vocab.definition: painful and uncomfortable, especially a throat or muscle
vocab.example: She woke up with a sore throat and a headache.

vocab.definition: unable to pass air or liquid through normally
vocab.example: She had a blocked nose and couldn't breathe well.

vocab.definition: the regular beating of blood through your heart and body
vocab.example: The nurse took her temperature, blood pressure, and pulse.

grammarNote: "Have got" — это разговорный вариант глагола "have", очень распространённый в британском английском. Используется для описания того, ЧТО У ТЕБЯ ЕСТЬ, включая части тела, симптомы болезни и физические характеристики. Важно: have got = have (то же значение, но другая форма).

rows.form: Use have (NOT have got) for actions
rows.example: I have breakfast at 7 am. (NOT "I've got breakfast") ❌

rows.form: have got — more common in British English
rows.example: British: I've got a problem. American: I have a problem.

rows.form: Questions: Have you got? or Do you have?
rows.example: Both correct: Have you got a pen? = Do you have a pen?

grammarTip:
have got = have (то же значение!):
→ I've got a headache. = I have a headache. ✅
→ She's got brown eyes. = She has brown eyes. ✅

НО! Для ДЕЙСТВИЙ используй только have (не have got):
→ I have breakfast at 7. ✅ (не 'I've got breakfast') ❌
→ I have a shower every morning. ✅

В разговорной речи have got звучит естественнее. В British English особенно популярно!
